name: Trotula medieval cosmetic text

card.summary: A set of 12th-century Salernitan texts on women's medicine that includes De ornatu mulierum, the earliest known Western cosmetic treatise, with recipes for skin, hair, teeth and body care.
card.note: Historical recipes use ingredients such as alum and animal products; they are documented as history, not as guidance.

quick.overview:
The Trotula is the name given to three Latin texts on women's health written in Salerno, southern Italy, in the 12th century. One of them, De ornatu mulierum (On Women's Cosmetics), is a beauty handbook covering hair, skin, face, lips, teeth and mouth care.

For appearance, it is a historical window: it shows what medieval women used to soften skin, remove hair, colour hair and whiten teeth, and modern dermatology papers have compared its formulas with today's cosmetics. Nearly 200 manuscripts survive, so it circulated widely.
quick.how: Readers today encounter it as history, translated editions and scholarly comparisons rather than as a routine. In its own era, recipes used plants, minerals, animal products and imported spices applied as washes, ointments, powders and steam baths. Modern authors compare these with current skincare in journals.
quick.risks: The medieval ingredients include substances such as alum and animal products, and some historical cosmetic ingredients elsewhere in history were toxic, so the recipes are documented rather than recommended. Authorship is debated: the cosmetic text is not generally attributed to the physician Trota herself.

lead: The Trotula is a name for three 12th-century Latin texts on women's medicine written in Salerno: the Liber de sinthomatibus mulierum (conditions of women), De curis mulierum (treatments for women) and De ornatu mulierum (women's cosmetics).[1][5] The name comes from Trota of Salerno, a historical practitioner linked to one of the texts, though medieval readers often treated Trotula as a single woman author.[5]

De ornatu mulierum is the part relevant to appearance. It covers care of the hair (including body hair), face, lips, teeth and mouth, using imported spices such as frankincense, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg and galangal, and it includes a steam bath for women without access to spas.[5] It is described as the earliest known dedicated cosmetic treatise in Western medicine, with formulas for dyes, depilatories, freckle removers and hair products.[1]

Modern dermatology and cosmetic-science journals revisit the text: a 2008 paper calls it the first cosmetic treatise of history from a female point of view,[2] and a 2023 paper critically compares its medieval skincare formulations with modern dermocosmetics.[3]

angle.text: The cosmetic text records what medieval women did to improve skin, hair and teeth, and modern authors compare it with today's skincare. It is read mostly as history.

paras: Salerno's medical school was an early centre of European medicine, flourishing from the 10th to 13th centuries, where women took part as teachers and students.[2][4] The Trotula texts emerged from this environment, drawing on Greek, Arabic and Latin sources.[1]

Scholars attribute only De curis mulierum to Trota in its earliest form, and Monica Green argues she is best understood as the authority behind it; John Benton showed in 1985 that the printed edition merged three separate texts.[5]

De ornatu mulierum is the shortest of the three. It addresses preventive hygiene and beautification in sections on hair, skin, teeth and nails, offering dyes, depilatories, freckle removers and hair restoratives with substances such as alum, saffron and goat's blood, and it opens with a defence against charges of vanity.[1] Wikipedia notes it credits six practices to Muslim women.[5]
Dental care in the Salerno school is covered in a separate paper describing oral hygiene precepts and specific dental practices.[6]

Nearly 200 manuscripts survive, over 130 in Latin and over 60 in vernacular languages, and translations include Hebrew, Anglo-Norman, Old French, Dutch, Middle English, German, Irish and Italian.[5] In 1544 Johannes Schottus and Georg Kraut printed the texts as one work; in 1566 Hans Caspar Wolf renamed the author Eros, and in the 20th century Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party popularised Trotula.[5]

The 2023 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology paper applied a historical-critical method to the Latin text and an English translation to compare medieval and modern dermocosmetics.[3] A 2019 paper in the same journal reviews the medical dermatology and cosmetic treatises ascribed to Trotula de Ruggiero.[7]
No studies found. The literature is historical and comparative rather than clinical.[3][7]
